name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Tuesday 15 September 1981

clue.text: Felicitate count, at large after liberation

indicators.note: once liberated, the letters are free to wander and settle in a fresh order

blocks.note: the twelve letters of these two words are the raw material

explanation.surface: A count escapes captivity and someone hurries to wish him well on his freedom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At large' looks like it describes the freed count, but its letters are part of the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To felicitate someone is to offer them good wishes on their success, a formal synonym.

clue.text: Spotted hunter, as leaving chase with rising loathing

indicators.note: the first word leaving means those two letters depart from the word that follows
in a down clue, rising means read from bottom to top, so the word is taken backwards

blocks.note: taken as written, before two of its letters leave
hate is loathing

explanation.surface: A spotted predator gives up its pursuit, filled with growing disgust.
explanation.definitionFit: The cheetah is a big cat with a spotted coat that hunts by running down its prey.

clue.text: Nor yet what may be made therein

indicators.note: something made from given material is a new construction, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: the seven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned legal phrase about something not yet made inside some place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nor yet' is an old phrase meaning 'and not either'; 'what may be made' asks what other word can be built from the last word's letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Both expressions introduce a further negative alternative, as in 'not this, nor yet that', the role of a negative conjunction.

clue.text: Driver's signal just about in good time? Not quite!

indicators.note: about means around, so one word goes round the other
not quite means falling a little short, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: just means right or fair
early means in good time

explanation.surface: A motorist signals just in time, though not quite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not quite' trims only the word right before it, the one for 'in good time'.
explanation.definitionFit: The red lamp at the back of a car warns following traffic, a signal from the driver to others on the road.

clue.text: I had the favourite up first, Laodicean

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from bottom to top, so the word is taken backwards
first places the backward favourite ahead of the contraction

blocks.note: a pet is a favourite
I'd is the contraction of I had

explanation.surface: A punter says he backed the favourite early on, but feels half-hearted about it.
explanation.walkthrough: Laodicean means half-hearted, from the church at Laodicea rebuked in Revelation for being 'neither cold nor hot'.
explanation.definitionFit: Laodicean describes lukewarm indifference, especially in religion or politics; the Bible's 'lukewarm' church gave the word.

clue.text: Bounty, a great ship

blocks.note: large means great in size
SS, steamship, is the standard ship abbreviation

explanation.surface: HMS Bounty, of mutiny fame, is called a mighty vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bounty was the ship of the famous 1789 mutiny, which makes it look like the topic; here 'Bounty' is generosity.
explanation.definitionFit: Largess is generous giving of money or gifts, so it means bounty in the sense of liberality.

clue.text: Is one surrounded by fish in this country?

indicators.note: surrounded by means enclosed within, so the first pieces sit inside the fish

blocks.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one
a tuna is a fish

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about whether a person is hemmed in by fish within some nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Tunisia is a North African country on the Mediterranean coast, the nation the question refers to.

clue.text: His mirth is killing

blocks.note: his means belonging to a man, a man's
mirth is laughter

explanation.surface: Someone's laughter is so funny it is killing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Killing' looks like slang for hilarious, but it is the noun for taking a life.
explanation.definitionFit: Manslaughter is the legal term for unlawfully killing someone without malice aforethought.

clue.text: Girl declares her name where Wilde declared his genius

blocks.note: introducing herself, she says 'I am ...'
a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl introduces herself at the very spot where Oscar Wilde made his famous boast.
explanation.walkthrough: Arriving in New York in 1882, Oscar Wilde reputedly told customs officers he had nothing to declare but his genius. The girl says 'I am Erica'.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilde's legendary customs quip was made on landing in the United States, so the country is the place described.

clue.text: Fixes the blame on retiring radical for eating

indicators.note: something retiring draws back, so the phrase before it is taken backwards

blocks.note: to fix the blame on someone is to 'pin the rap on' them; 'pins rap' is the phrase used here

explanation.surface: Someone blames a retreating extremist for a meal he has eaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Radical' looks like the political extremist, but it is the botanical sense: of the root.
explanation.definitionFit: Radical literally means relating to a root; the parsnip is a root vegetable grown to be eaten.

clue.text: Possibly coming in by river

blocks.note: per means by, as in per post
an advent is an arrival or coming
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: Someone might perhaps be arriving along a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Blocks are read in a different order from the clue: the 'by' word goes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Peradventure is an archaic adverb meaning perhaps or by chance, so it means possibly.

clue.text: Flowers at Chelsea completely hide their container

indicators.note: the words before it conceal the answer whole within their run of letters

blocks.note: read straight through the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Blooms at the Chelsea Flower Show are packed so densely they cover their pots.
explanation.walkthrough: The Chelsea Flower Show is a famous annual London garden show, which makes 'Flowers' look like the topic.
explanation.definitionFit: A satchel is a bag with a strap for carrying books, so it is a kind of container.

clue.text: Valet's part of the furniture

blocks.note: first meaning: a person who helps another put on clothes
second meaning: a sideboard or kitchen cabinet with shelves

explanation.surface: A manservant is so long in post he is treated like part of the furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: A valet's job includes helping his employer get clothed, and the same word names a cabinet with shelves for dishes.

clue.text: Regard sailor with horror? Not half!

definitions.note: the full sense is 'regard with horror'; the last words also serve the wordplay

indicators.note: not half means only half of the word before it is kept, the rest discarded

blocks.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is the usual crossword sailor
taken as written before it is cut down

explanation.surface: Someone eyes a seaman with dread, then insists it was not that bad at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is really 'regard with horror', and 'horror' does double duty, also supplying its first half.
explanation.definitionFit: To abhor something is to detest it utterly, which is exactly looking upon it with horror.

clue.text: Donkey left in very good pasture

indicators.note: in places the beast and the side inside the words that follow

blocks.note: a donkey is an ass
L is the standard abbreviation for left
grand means splendid or excellent

explanation.surface: A donkey has been turned out into an excellent field.
explanation.definitionFit: Grassland is open land covered in grass, the kind animals graze on, so a synonym for pasture.

clue.text: Coquette, losing footing, goes head first into a little water butt

indicators.note: in a down clue the foot is the last letter, so the word sheds its final letter
going head first in a down clue means upside down, so the word is turned backwards
into means entering, so the upturned word is put inside what follows

blocks.note: taken as written
a pool is a small body of water
a coquette is a flirt

explanation.surface: A flirtatious woman slips and tumbles headlong into a rain barrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water butt' looks like one item, a rain barrel; 'butt' alone is the definition, meaning the target of a joke.
explanation.definitionFit: An April fool is the victim of a prank played on 1 April, so the butt of the joke.

clue.text: Fighter pleased with the list I brought back

indicators.note: brought back means carried the return way, so the words before it are read in reverse

blocks.note: glad means pleased
a rota is a list of duties
taken as written

explanation.surface: A combatant is delighted when the roster he submitted is returned to him.
explanation.definitionFit: A gladiator was an armed combatant who fought in the Roman arena, so a fighter by profession.

clue.text: Girl, given Chinese food, wanting more

blocks.note: a girl's name
rice is the staple of Chinese meals

explanation.surface: A girl is served a Chinese meal and still asks for seconds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanting more' reads as hungry for seconds, but it is a noun phrase: the state of always wanting more.
explanation.definitionFit: Avarice is greed for wealth, a constant craving for more than one already has.

clue.text: Tooth in Cophetua's head is gold

indicators.note: the head of a name is its opening letter

blocks.note: taken as written
the king's name supplies only its opening letter
taken as written
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: King Cophetua, the legendary African king who wed a beggar maid, has a gold tooth.
explanation.definitionFit: An incisor is one of the flat cutting teeth at the front of the mouth.

clue.text: Taxi, the French means of. . communication'

blocks.note: a cab is a taxi
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A French taxi is described as a way of getting a message across.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray dots and apostrophe are scanning debris in the newspaper copy; the definition is simply 'means of communication'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cable was a telegram sent along an undersea wire, once a standard way to send a message abroad.

clue.text: Little bird of mine?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone fondly calls a small bird their own
setter's reading: a small bird whose name begins with the fuel dug from a pit

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mine' looks like the possessive, but it is the pit where fuel is dug; a tit is a little bird, and this one is named for that fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: The coal tit is a small European songbird with a black cap, one of the tit family.

clue.text: Dance with nothing on - swell!

blocks.note: a ball is a formal dance
O looks like zero, nothing
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone cheers a party where the dancers wear no clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swell!' reads as an exclamation of approval, but it is the verb meaning to expand.
explanation.definitionFit: To balloon is to swell up or expand rapidly, like a balloon being inflated.

clue.text: Sleeps - can rest only fitfully

indicators.note: fitfully means in irregular bursts, so the letters lie in a disordered arrangement

blocks.note: the seven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An insomniac complains that he dozes but never properly settles.
explanation.definitionFit: Trances are dreamlike states of suspended awareness, close enough to slumbers to stand for them.

clue.text: Cleaner oar

blocks.note: first meaning: a chimney cleaner
second meaning: a long oar used for steering or rowing

explanation.definitionFit: A chimney cleaner is known by this name, and a long oar worked by one rower is called the same.

clue.text: Tract hired out to a retiring pixy

indicators.note: a retiring figure draws back, so the little sprite is written backwards
the hire word is pushed to around the rest, closing on it like a door pulled to

blocks.note: property let out is hired out to tenants
taken as written
a pixy is a small sprite or elf

explanation.surface: A stretch of land is rented to a shy little sprite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tract' looks like a stretch of land, but it is the printed pamphlet. The placement signal is loose: the backward sprite with its article sits inside the rental word.
explanation.definitionFit: A tract is a short pamphlet, usually religious or political, and a leaflet is a printed sheet of the same kind.

clue.text: New edition is about a little island girl

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
Is. is the abbreviation for island
a girl's name

explanation.surface: A fresh printing tells the story of a girl from a small island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A little island' means an abbreviated one, not a small one.
explanation.definitionFit: A reissue is a book or record published again, so it is a new edition of an existing work.

clue.text: Excel alternatively in these sports

definitions.note: the answer is the adjective that describes these sports

blocks.note: to outdo is to surpass or excel
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: Someone could shine in this kind of sport, or perhaps another.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads with the answer as 'outdoor sports': the clue points at the kind of sport rather than naming it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sports such as cricket, golf and hiking are played in the open air, so they are called outdoor sports.

clue.text: Bishop Latimer on top form

indicators.note: to form something is to shape it, so the letters are moulded into a new arrangement

blocks.note: the twelve letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Bishop Hugh Latimer, the Tudor martyr, is said to be at his very best.
explanation.walkthrough: Hugh Latimer really was a bishop, burned at Oxford in 1555, so 'Bishop Latimer' reads as one name; 'on top form' must be broken apart too.
explanation.definitionFit: A metropolitan is a senior bishop presiding over a province of dioceses, an archbishop in all but name.
